distractors: describing conduct that is wrong only because a statute happens to forbid it
describing an act that is legal in some jurisdictions but not others

example.text: Murder is considered malum in se, wrong by its very nature rather than merely by law.

en.correct: an act that is criminal only because a statute prohibits it, not because it is inherently immoral
distractors: an act that is inherently evil regardless of legislation
a crime punishable only by a fine, never imprisonment

example.text: Failing to obtain the required permit is malum prohibitum rather than inherently wrongful conduct.

en.correct: the doctrine under which the state acts as guardian for individuals who cannot protect their own interests, such as children
distractors: the rule that parents are strictly liable for their children's torts
a court's authority to appoint an executor for an estate

example.text: The state sued the manufacturer in its parens patriae capacity to protect the interests of its residents.

en.correct: acting in the role and with the legal authority of a parent, typically applied to schools or guardians
distractors: acting entirely without legal authority over a minor
describing a custody arrangement ordered temporarily by a court

example.text: As the school stood in loco parentis during the field trip, it owed the students a duty of care.

en.correct: an equitable doctrine allowing a court to redirect funds or a charitable gift toward a purpose as close as possible to the original intent when that intent becomes impossible or impractical
distractors: the doctrine allowing a will to be entirely rewritten by the court
a rule requiring settlements to be split equally among class members

example.text: The court applied the cy pres doctrine to distribute the unclaimed settlement funds to a related charity.

en.correct: an equitable defense barring a claim because the plaintiff unreasonably delayed in asserting it, causing prejudice to the other party
distractors: the statutory deadline by which any lawsuit must be filed
a rule limiting how much a jury may award in damages

example.text: The court barred the claim under laches because the plaintiff waited decades to assert his rights while evidence was lost.

en.correct: an equitable defense barring relief for a plaintiff who has acted unethically or in bad faith regarding the matter in dispute
distractors: a rule disqualifying a juror who has a criminal record
the requirement that all parties be represented by counsel

example.text: The court refused to grant the injunction because the plaintiff came to it with unclean hands.

en.correct: the suspension or pausing of the running of a statute of limitations during a specified period
distractors: the permanent forfeiture of a claim once the limitations period expires
a court's authority to shorten a limitations period at its discretion

example.text: The limitations period was tolled while the defendant was out of the state and could not be served.

en.correct: the doctrine that courts should generally follow established precedent when deciding similar cases
distractors: the principle that a legislature may retroactively overturn any judicial decision
the rule requiring unanimous agreement among appellate judges

example.text: Even justices skeptical of the earlier ruling hesitated to overturn it, citing stare decisis.

en.correct: the standing requirement that a favorable court decision must be likely to remedy the plaintiff's injury
distractors: the requirement that damages be calculated with mathematical precision
the rule that only monetary relief may be awarded in federal court

example.text: The suit failed on redressability because a ruling for the plaintiff would not have stopped the harm.

en.correct: describing a treaty or constitutional provision that takes effect as domestic law without the need for further implementing legislation
distractors: describing a law that automatically expires after five years
describing a court order that a party may ignore without penalty

example.text: The court held the treaty provision was self-executing and therefore enforceable without an implementing statute.

en.correct: invalid from the very outset, as though it never had any legal effect
distractors: valid until formally challenged in court
enforceable only after a court's later ratification

example.text: The court declared the fraudulently obtained contract void ab initio.

en.correct: having retroactive legal effect, as if an order or filing had occurred at an earlier date
distractors: applicable only to future proceedings, never retroactively
issued without any written record

example.text: The judge entered the corrected order nunc pro tunc to the original filing date.

en.correct: anew, as if for the first time, without deference to a prior decision-maker's conclusions
distractors: with substantial deference to the original decision-maker
only with respect to factual, not legal, determinations

example.text: The appellate court reviewed the purely legal question de novo.

en.correct: existing in practice or fact, regardless of official legal recognition
distractors: existing only by explicit statutory authorization
recognized formally but never actually implemented

example.text: Despite lacking formal authority, he had become the de facto head of the agency.

en.correct: existing by operation of law or formal legal recognition, as opposed to mere practice
distractors: existing informally, without any legal basis
recognized only by international custom, never domestic law

example.text: The court distinguished de jure segregation, mandated by law, from mere de facto patterns of separation.

en.correct: describing a court's jurisdiction over the person of a specific defendant, rather than over property
distractors: describing jurisdiction over property located within the court's territory
describing a judgment that binds the whole world

example.text: The court lacked in personam jurisdiction because the defendant had no meaningful contacts with the state.

en.correct: describing a court's jurisdiction over a specific piece of property, rather than over a particular person
distractors: describing jurisdiction based solely on the defendant's citizenship
describing a criminal proceeding brought against a corporation

example.text: The forfeiture proceeding was an in rem action against the seized vessel itself.

en.correct: describing an executive or administrative function that resembles a court's role of adjudicating disputes and applying rules to facts
distractors: describing a purely legislative function involving no factfinding
describing an action taken exclusively by a jury

example.text: The zoning board exercised a quasi-judicial function when it held hearings and ruled on the variance.

en.correct: describing an administrative agency's function of creating generally applicable rules, resembling the lawmaking role of a legislature
distractors: describing a court's power to interpret a statute's plain meaning
describing the exclusively enforcement-related duties of an agency

example.text: The agency's quasi-legislative rulemaking established binding standards for the entire industry.

en.correct: on its own initiative, without a request or motion from either party
distractors: only after a formal motion filed by one of the parties
exclusively at the direction of an appellate court

example.text: The judge raised the jurisdictional defect sua sponte, without either party mentioning it.

en.correct: in private, in a judge's chambers or otherwise outside public view
distractors: in open court, before the assembled public
by written submission only, without any hearing

example.text: The judge reviewed the disputed documents in camera before ruling on the privilege claim.

en.correct: describing a court opinion issued in the name of the court as a whole rather than attributed to a single authoring judge
distractors: describing an opinion that carries no binding legal effect
describing a ruling issued exclusively by a single trial judge

example.text: The unsigned per curiam opinion resolved the case without identifying its author.

en.correct: describing an act performed beyond the scope of legal authority or power granted to the actor
distractors: describing an act performed within the clear scope of one's authority
describing conduct that is criminal but not civilly actionable

example.text: The board's contract was voided as ultra vires because it exceeded the corporation's chartered powers.

en.correct: describing a law that retroactively criminalizes conduct or increases punishment for an act already committed
distractors: describing a law that applies only prospectively to future conduct
describing a law passed unanimously by the legislature

example.text: The statute increasing penalties for past conduct was struck down as an unconstitutional ex post facto law.

en.correct: capable of being resolved by a court because it presents a genuine, concrete legal dispute appropriate for judicial decision
distractors: resolvable only through legislative action, never by courts
requiring unanimous consent of all parties before a court may hear it

example.text: The court found the dispute justiciable and proceeded to decide the merits.

en.correct: sufficient by itself to determine the outcome of an issue or an entire case
distractors: merely persuasive but never determinative of a case's outcome
applicable only to procedural, not substantive, matters

example.text: The signed waiver proved dispositive, ending the case without a trial.

en.correct: no longer presenting a live controversy, such that a court's decision would have no practical effect
distractors: presenting a controversy so urgent that it demands immediate review
involving facts that are still genuinely disputed by the parties

example.text: The appeal became moot once the challenged policy was voluntarily withdrawn.

en.correct: tending to prove or disprove a fact at issue, and therefore relevant to a case
distractors: certain to persuade a jury regardless of other evidence
inadmissible because it was obtained through improper means

example.text: The judge admitted the photograph because it was highly probative of the defendant's location.

en.correct: tending to clear a defendant of guilt or fault
distractors: tending to establish a defendant's guilt beyond doubt
relevant only to sentencing, not to guilt

example.text: The prosecution was required to disclose the exculpatory evidence to the defense before trial.

en.correct: tending to indicate or establish a person's guilt or involvement in wrongdoing
distractors: tending to excuse a defendant from criminal responsibility
relevant only to civil, not criminal, proceedings

example.text: The inculpatory text messages were introduced to link the defendant to the scheme.

en.correct: describing evidence whose potential to unfairly bias the factfinder outweighs its legitimate value
distractors: describing evidence that is always excluded regardless of context
describing testimony given under oath by an expert witness

example.text: The court excluded the graphic photographs as unfairly prejudicial and only marginally relevant.

en.correct: describing a court order or ruling issued during litigation that does not finally resolve the entire case
distractors: describing the single order that concludes a case on the merits
describing a ruling that can never be appealed under any circumstances

example.text: The interlocutory order denying summary judgment was not immediately appealable.

en.correct: capable of being separated from the rest of an agreement or statute so that the remainder can survive independently
distractors: incapable of being enforced under any circumstances
binding only on the parties who negotiated the original terms

example.text: The illegal clause was severable, leaving the rest of the contract enforceable.

en.correct: describing a speech regulation that applies regardless of the topic or message being expressed
distractors: describing a law that singles out particular viewpoints for restriction
describing a regulation that applies only to government speech

example.text: The noise ordinance was content-neutral because it restricted volume regardless of the message conveyed.

en.correct: closely related or relevant to the matter at hand, as required for an amendment to be permissible under legislative procedure
distractors: entirely unrelated to the subject under discussion
binding only after formal adoption by a committee

example.text: The Senate rule required that any floor amendment be germane to the underlying bill.

en.correct: to arrange and compile scattered laws or rules into an organized, systematic legal code
distractors: to formally repeal an existing statute
to submit a legal dispute to binding arbitration

example.text: Congress voted to codify the agency's longstanding practice into permanent statutory law.

en.correct: to formally issue or put into effect a law, rule, or regulation
distractors: to permanently strike down a law as unconstitutional
to privately negotiate a settlement between disputing parties

example.text: The agency promulgated the new safety regulations after a lengthy notice-and-comment period.

en.correct: to formally abolish or repeal a law, right, or agreement
distractors: to temporarily suspend a rule pending further review
to expand the scope of an existing right

example.text: The treaty was abrogated when the government formally withdrew from it.

en.correct: to hear and formally resolve a legal dispute through the judicial process
distractors: to informally mediate a dispute outside of court
to draft legislation on behalf of a client

example.text: The tribunal was created to adjudicate claims arising from the disputed territory.

en.correct: to bring a criminal defendant before a court to hear the formal charges and enter a plea
distractors: to formally sentence a defendant after conviction
to summon a witness to testify before a grand jury

example.text: The defendant was arraigned the morning after his arrest and pleaded not guilty.

en.correct: to formally charge a public official with misconduct as the first step toward removal from office, or to challenge a witness's credibility
distractors: to permanently remove an official from office without any further proceeding
to pardon an official for prior misconduct

example.text: The House voted to impeach the official, sending the matter to the Senate for trial.

en.correct: to legally prohibit or compel a party to act through a court's injunctive order
distractors: to voluntarily agree to a settlement without court involvement
to formally join two lawsuits into a single proceeding

example.text: The court enjoined the company from continuing the deceptive advertising practice.

en.correct: to set aside or annul a judgment, order, or decision, rendering it legally void
distractors: to uphold a lower court's ruling in full
to postpone a scheduled trial to a later date

example.text: The appellate court vacated the conviction and remanded the case for a new trial.

en.correct: to send a case back to a lower court or agency for further proceedings consistent with the reviewing court's decision
distractors: to permanently dismiss a case with prejudice
to consolidate multiple related cases into one

example.text: The Supreme Court remanded the case to the circuit court to apply the newly announced standard.

en.correct: to argue that a precedent does not control the current case because of relevant factual or legal differences
distractors: to formally overturn a prior precedent
to certify a case for review by a higher court

example.text: Defense counsel sought to distinguish the unfavorable precedent based on the different statutory language at issue.
